segments.title: About the mastery check
segments.body: This check has new questions on every objective. Your report shows each objective separately: **met independently**, **met with support** (if you used hint 3 or 4), or **not yet**. You're ready for the lecture when nothing is “not yet”. If something is, you'll get a short review and a fresh set of questions for it.

review_segments.title: Review: Data structures, algorithms, graphs and traversals
review_segments.body:
A **data structure** stores data (a queue, a dictionary, a graph). An **algorithm** is a list of steps (BFS, sorting). A **graph** is vertices joined by edges. A **graph traversal** visits the vertices by following edges, and BFS is one.

**Go back to:** Module 1, segments 2 and 3 (video “From a map to a graph” and “Key terms”).

review_segments.title: Review practice: data structures, algorithms, graphs and traversals
Review: Vertices, edges and direction
review_segments.body:
**Vertices** are the circles (the things). **Edges** are the lines (the connections), named by their two ends. If edges have **arrows**, the graph is **directed**; plain lines mean **undirected**. Two arrows between the same pair still make it directed.

**Go back to:** Module 1, segments 4, 5, 7 and 8 (worked example, labelling, “One-way or two-way?”, classifying).

review_segments.title: Review practice: vertices, edges and direction
Review: Modelling a real situation as a graph
review_segments.body:
Ask three questions. What are the **things**? They're the vertices. What **connects** them? Those are the edges. Does each connection work **both ways**? If not, the graph is directed.

**Go back to:** Module 1, segments 6 and 9 (building the campus graph and “Graphs in real life”).

review_segments.title: Review practice: modelling a real situation as a graph
Review: When BFS is the right tool
review_segments.body:
BFS is good for two jobs: finding the route with the **fewest edges**, and finding **everything reachable** from a start. It isn't for problems without connections, or where edges have different costs or lengths.

**Go back to:** Module 3, segments 3 and 4 (video “Why BFS?” and “When is BFS the right tool?”).

review_segments.title: Review practice: when bfs is the right tool
Review: Tracing BFS by hand
review_segments.body:
Each step: take the vertex at the **front** of the queue; add its unvisited neighbours to the **back**, in alphabetical order; mark them **visited** as they join. Repeat until the queue is empty.

**Go back to:** Module 3, segments 5 to 8 (video “BFS step by step”, prediction, worked trace table, trace practice).

review_segments.title: Review practice: tracing bfs by hand
Review: Writing BFS in Python
review_segments.body:
Before the loop: `visited = {start}`, `queue = deque([start])`, `order = []`. In the loop: `v = queue.popleft()`, `order.append(v)`, then for each `n` in `sorted(graph.adjacency[v])`, if it isn't visited, add it to `visited` and `queue`. Return `order`.

**Go back to:** Module 4, segments 4 to 7 (worked example, Parsons, fill-in, writing BFS).

review_segments.title: Review practice: writing bfs in python
Review: Testing and debugging BFS
review_segments.body:
A good test builds a small graph, calls `bfs`, and asserts the **exact** list it should return. Two graphs catch most BFS bugs: one with a **cycle** (catches vertices visited twice) and one that's **disconnected** (catches vertices that shouldn't be reached).

**Go back to:** Module 5 (Test and debug).
